content:
Every black hole hides a question at its center. Einstein's theory predicts that whatever falls in is crushed into a singularity, a point of infinite density where the theory itself breaks down. Most physicists expect quantum ...

One answer is to listen. A disturbed black hole, for instance, one just born from a merger, rings like a struck bell, shedding gravitational waves in a few quickly fading tones that physicists call quasinormal modes. Each tone has a pitch and a fading rate, set by the shape of spacetime around the black hole. Build the center differently, and the black hole should ring differently.

Over the past year, my colleague Davide Batic and I, with Fabio Scardigli for the first two papers, computed these tones for three black holes whose centers are reshaped by ideas from quantum gravity. Our third paper, now published in Physics of the Dark Universe, completes the series, and the answers fall into a simple pattern: where gravity weakens at short distances, the black hole rings higher and longer; where it grows stronger, it rings lower and dies away sooner.

Gravity that changes with distance

In Newton's and Einstein's theories, one number, Newton's constant, fixes the strength of gravity. Several approaches to quantum gravity suggest that it depends on distance. In asymptotic safety, an idea due to Steven Weinberg, gravity weakens at the very shortest distances. Put such a running constant into Einstein's black hole, and its center changes.

In our first paper, in The European Physical Journal C, the constant follows the quantum correction to Newton's law, and gravity grows stronger near the center. The singularity survives, but it is spread over a sphere, the edge of a core of Planck density, still hidden behind the horizon.

Three black holes with reshaped centers, each struck once, and the main gravitational tone it rings (in color), drawn over the tone of Einstein's black hole of the same mass (gray). The Planck star, where gravity grows stronger near the center, rings lower and dies away after 1.9 oscillations instead of 3.1. The Bonanno–Reuter and Hayward black holes at their extreme points, where gravity weakens, ring higher and keep ringing for 4.4 and 4.3 oscillations. The dotted marks show when each tone has fallen to 1% of its first swing. Time is in units of the black hole's mass, and each curve is a single tone with the pitch and the fading rate computed in our papers. Credit: Denys Dutykh

How strong gravity is at each distance from the center, compared with Newton's constant, for the three black holes compared in our third paper. In Einstein's theory it is the same everywhere (gray line). In the Planck star it grows near the center and becomes infinite on the singular sphere (dotted line). In the extreme Bonanno–Reuter and Hayward black holes, whose curves almost coincide, it weakens and switches off at the center. Circles mark the event horizons and diamonds the light rings, where the ringing is made. Distances are in units of the black hole's mass. Credit: Denys Dutykh

Spacetime (Penrose) diagrams of the three kinds of black hole, in which time runs upward, light travels at 45 degrees and infinity is drawn at a finite distance. Left, the Planck star: whatever crosses the event horizon still ends on a singularity, but a sphere rather than a point. Middle, the Bonanno–Reuter and Hayward black holes: the singularity gives way to a smooth core, behind a second, inner horizon. Right, their extreme case, where the two horizons merge. In all three, a pulse strikes the light ring (red band), and the ringing travels out to a distant observer. Credit: Denys Dutykh

The main gravitational tone in the plane of pitch and fading rate, both in units of the black hole's mass. Each path starts from Einstein's black hole (black dot) and follows one family as its core grows: the Planck star of one Planck mass, the Bonanno–Reuter black hole as its mass falls to the extreme value of 3.50 Planck masses, and the Hayward black hole as its core parameter grows to 32/27. The Planck star moves up and to the left, to a lower tone that fades faster. The two others move down and to the right, to a higher tone that rings longer. Credit: Denys Dutykh

Why the pitch moves: four black holes of the same mass drawn to scale, with radii in units of the mass. The ringing is made at the light ring (dashed), where light can circle the black hole. In the Planck star the ring sits 38% farther out than in Einstein's black hole, waves circle it more slowly, and the main tone is 25% lower. In the extreme Bonanno–Reuter and Hayward black holes the ring sits 14% and 12% closer in, and the tone is 12% and 9.5% higher. Credit: Denys Dutykh
